question.prompt:
How many ordered triples of integers \((x, y, z)\) satisfy the following system of inequalities?

\[-x - y - z \le -2\] \[-x + y + z \le 2\] \[x - y + z \le 2\] \[x + y - z \le 2\]

solutions.title: Bound the coordinates
solutions.explanation:
Adding pairs of inequalities cancels two variables, which will leave only a few possible values for each coordinate.

Adding the first two inequalities gives
\[
-2x\le 0,
\]
so \(x\ge 0\). Adding the last two gives \(2x\le 4\), so \(x\le 2\). By symmetry, the same bounds hold for \(y\) and \(z\). Thus every coordinate belongs to \(\{0,1,2\}\).

We now classify triples by their smallest coordinate. The inequalities are unchanged when coordinates are permuted.

If a coordinate is \(0\), put it in the first position. The first two inequalities then give \(y+z\ge 2\) and \(y+z\le 2\), so \(y+z=2\). The possible patterns are therefore \((0,0,2)\) and \((0,1,1)\).

If the smallest coordinate is \(1\), put it first. The inequality \(-1+y+z\le 2\) gives \(y+z\le 3\). Since both remaining coordinates are \(1\) or \(2\), the possible patterns are \((1,1,1)\) and \((1,1,2)\).

If the smallest coordinate is \(2\), all three coordinates are \(2\). Substitution confirms that each listed pattern satisfies every inequality.

| Smallest coordinate | Patterns, before reordering | Number of ordered triples |
|---|---|---:|
| \(0\) | \((0,0,2),\ (0,1,1)\) | \(3+3=6\) |
| \(1\) | \((1,1,1),\ (1,1,2)\) | \(1+3=4\) |
| \(2\) | \((2,2,2)\) | \(1\) |

A pattern with two equal entries has three reorderings, determined by the position of its different entry. A pattern with all entries equal has one. The cases are disjoint and cover every possible smallest coordinate, so the total is
\[
6+4+1=\boxed{11},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Change variables and use parity
solutions.explanation:
The last three left-hand sides can serve as new variables, making three of the bounds especially simple. Define
\[
p=-x+y+z,\qquad q=x-y+z,\qquad r=x+y-z.
\]
Then \(p,q,r\le 2\), and
\[
p+q+r=x+y+z\ge 2.
\]
Each new variable is also at least \(-2\): for example, \(p\ge 2-q-r\ge -2\).

The pairwise sums satisfy
\[
q+r=2x,\qquad p+r=2y,\qquad p+q=2z.
\]
Thus \(p,q,r\) must all have the same parity. Conversely, any integers of common parity with each in \([-2,2]\) and sum at least \(2\) give a unique integer triple through
\[
x=\frac{q+r}{2},\qquad y=\frac{p+r}{2},\qquad z=\frac{p+q}{2}.
\]
Substitution shows that these formulas recover the original inequalities, so counting the new triples counts the original ones exactly once.

If the new variables are even, their possible values are \(-2,0,2\). If a \(-2\) occurs, the other two entries must both be \(2\) to make the sum at least \(2\). Otherwise, all entries are \(0\) or \(2\), with at least one \(2\). This gives the complete list:

| Even pattern | Distinct reorderings |
|---|---:|
| \((2,2,2)\) | \(1\) |
| \((2,2,0)\) | \(3\) |
| \((2,0,0)\) | \(3\) |
| \((-2,2,2)\) | \(3\) |

The three reorderings in each applicable row correspond to the position of the different entry. There are \(10\) even triples.

If the variables are odd, each is \(-1\) or \(1\). Any \(-1\) would make the sum at most \(1\), so only \((1,1,1)\) works.

Therefore the number of original triples is
\[
10+1=\boxed{11},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
